newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai copper ends limit-down on panic selling.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai copper ends limit-down on panic selling.

text.p: Shanghai copper futures ended limit-down on Wednesday on panic selling following heavy overnight losses on the London Metal Exchange (LME), traders said.
The most actively traded November 1997 contract ended at 20,680 yuan ($2,494) per tonne, losing 500 yuan. It opened at 20,680 yuan and hit a high of 21,400 yuan per tonne.
July fell 590 to 21,490, August 550 to 20,600, September 580 to 20,620, October 480 to 20,670, and December 540 to 20,660. The first traded January 1998 contract ended at 20,600 yuan.
Combined volume rose to 91,655 tonnes from 66,660 tonnes.
The contracts opened at the limit-down level and moved at that level for most of the session.
Traders said panic selling dominated Wednesday's trade with few investors building new long positions.
"A large number of stop loss orders and fresh selling poured into the market, especially during the morning session," a trader said.
"Copper will maintain its downward trend in the next few days because market sentiment is extremely weak," he said.
The local physical price fell to 20,800 yuan, from 21,000 in the morning, chasing the futures market down, traders said.
Traders said they believed LME copper would keep falling in the short term, helping further weaken investor confidence in Shanghai.
In early Wednesday trading, LME copper was down $100 from the previous kerb close, nearing key support at $2,250 after triggering sell stops late on Tuesday.
At 0817 GMT, copper was at its lowest point since mid-April, at $2,263/2,268 per tonne. A stock rise of 975 tonnes was seen as unsupportive.
"Shanghai copper may find some support only at the key 20,000-yuan level," another local Shanghai trader said.
Aluminium ended mostly down. July fell 130 to 13,420, August rose 120 to 13,430, September dropped 220 to 13,500, October shed 380 to 13,500 and November lost 400 to 13,600 yuan per tonne.
Combined volume rose to 4,250 tonnes from 1,000 tonnes.
